little.say: This is your mouth. Big smile! You eat and talk with it.

young.what: Your mouth is where your food goes in.
young.does: Your teeth chew food, and your tongue helps you taste, swallow and talk.
young.funFact: Your mouth makes spit, called saliva, to help food slide down easily!

junior.what: The mouth, or oral cavity, is the start of the digestive system.
junior.does: Teeth break food into small pieces, saliva wets it and starts breaking down starch, and the tongue rolls it into a soft ball called a bolus for swallowing.
junior.funFact: People grow two sets of teeth: 20 milk teeth first, then 32 permanent teeth.
junior.details: Taste buds on your tongue detect sweet, salty, sour, bitter and savoury (umami) tastes.

bipc.definition: The oral (buccal) cavity is the first part of the alimentary canal, where mechanical digestion and the chemical digestion of starch begin.
bipc.structure: It contains the teeth, the tongue and the openings of three pairs of salivary glands (parotid, submandibular and sublingual). Human dentition is thecodont, diphyodont and heterodont; the adult dental formula is 2123/2123 (32 permanent teeth). The tongue is a freely movable muscular organ attached to the floor of the oral cavity by the frenulum, and its upper surface bears papillae, some of which carry taste buds.
bipc.function: Mastication breaks food into smaller pieces, and saliva moistens and lubricates it. Salivary amylase hydrolyses about 30% of starch into maltose at an optimum pH of about 6.8, and lysozyme in saliva acts as an antibacterial agent. The tongue shapes the food into a bolus, which is swallowed (deglutition).

keyTerms.meaning: Teeth embedded in sockets of the jaw bones
Two sets of teeth: milk (deciduous) and permanent
Enzyme in saliva that hydrolyses starch into maltose

syllabusRefs.topic: Digestive system: mouth and buccal cavity

chemistryLinks.explanation: Salivary amylase is a protein catalyst. Like all enzymes, it lowers the activation energy of a reaction and works best at an optimum pH and temperature.

flashcards.front: What is the adult human dental formula?

young.what: Your stomach is a stretchy bag inside your tummy.
young.does: It squishes and mixes food with special juices to break it down.
young.funFact: Your stomach stretches to hold a big meal, then shrinks back again!

junior.what: The stomach is a J-shaped, muscular organ in the upper left part of the abdomen.
junior.does: Its muscular walls churn food while gastric juice, which contains acid and enzymes, starts digesting proteins. The food becomes a thick liquid called chyme, which moves on into the small intestine.
junior.funFact: A layer of mucus stops the stomach's strong acid from harming its own lining.
junior.details: A ring of muscle called a sphincter at the lower end controls when food leaves the stomach.

bipc.definition: The stomach is a J-shaped, muscular dilation of the alimentary canal where food is stored for some hours and protein digestion begins.
bipc.structure: It is located in the upper left portion of the abdominal cavity and has a cardiac portion (into which the oesophagus opens), a fundic region, a body and a pyloric portion that opens into the duodenum. Its wall has the four layers of the alimentary canal: serosa, muscularis, sub-mucosa and mucosa. The mucosa forms gastric glands.
bipc.function: Gastric glands contain mucus neck cells (mucus), peptic or chief cells (pepsinogen) and parietal or oxyntic cells (HCl and intrinsic factor, needed to absorb vitamin B₁₂). HCl activates pepsinogen to pepsin and provides the acidic pH (about 1.8) that pepsin needs; pepsin converts proteins into proteoses and peptones. Churning mixes food with gastric juice to form chyme.

keyTerms.meaning: Parietal cells that secrete HCl and intrinsic factor
Inactive enzyme secreted by chief cells; activated to pepsin by HCl
Acidic, semi-liquid mixture of food and gastric juice

chemistryLinks.explanation: Gastric juice has a pH of about 1.8, so its hydrogen-ion concentration is roughly 10⁻¹·⁸ mol/L, strongly acidic.

young.what: Your liver is a big organ on the right side of your tummy, under your ribs.
young.does: It helps clean your blood and makes a juice called bile that helps digest fatty food.
young.funFact: Your liver can regrow parts of itself!

junior.what: The liver is the largest gland in the body, found in the upper right part of the abdomen.
junior.does: It makes bile, stores sugar as glycogen, removes harmful substances from the blood and makes important proteins.
junior.funFact: An adult liver weighs about 1.2 to 1.5 kilograms.
junior.details: Bile is stored in a small bag called the gallbladder and squeezed into the small intestine, where it breaks fat into tiny droplets.

bipc.definition: The liver is the largest gland of the body, weighing about 1.2–1.5 kg in an adult human, with digestive, metabolic and detoxifying roles.
bipc.structure: It lies in the abdominal cavity just below the diaphragm and has two lobes. The hepatic lobules are its structural and functional units; each contains hepatic cells arranged as cords and is covered by a thin connective tissue sheath called Glisson's capsule. Bile secreted by hepatic cells passes through the hepatic ducts and is stored and concentrated in the gallbladder; the cystic duct and the common hepatic duct join to form the common bile duct.
bipc.function: Bile contains bile salts, bile pigments (bilirubin and biliverdin), cholesterol and phospholipids but no enzymes; bile salts emulsify fats and help activate lipases. The liver also stores glycogen, produces urea from ammonia, detoxifies many substances and synthesises plasma proteins such as albumin and fibrinogen.

keyTerms.meaning: Structural and functional unit of the liver
Connective tissue sheath covering each hepatic lobule
Breaking fat into tiny droplets, increasing surface area for lipase

syllabusRefs.topic: Role of other organs in excretion

commonMistakes: Bile contains no digestive enzymes; it helps digestion by emulsifying fats.

young.what: Your food pipe is a long tube from your throat down to your stomach.
young.does: Its muscles squeeze to push food down, even if you are upside down!
young.funFact: Food takes only a few seconds to slide down to your stomach.

junior.what: The oesophagus is a muscular tube about 25 cm long that connects the throat (pharynx) to the stomach.
junior.does: Waves of muscle contraction, called peristalsis, push swallowed food down to the stomach.
junior.funFact: Thanks to peristalsis, astronauts can swallow food in space.
junior.details: A ring of muscle at its lower end stops stomach acid from coming back up.

young.what: Your small intestine is a long, twisty tube coiled up in your tummy.
young.does: It finishes breaking down food and soaks the goodness into your blood.
young.funFact: If you stretched it out, it would be longer than a car!

junior.what: The small intestine is a coiled tube about 6 metres long, made of the duodenum, jejunum and ileum.
junior.does: Juices from the pancreas and bile from the liver finish digesting food here, and millions of tiny finger-like villi absorb the nutrients into the blood.
junior.funFact: Its villi give it a huge inner surface, so it can absorb lots of nutrients quickly.
junior.details: It is called 'small' because it is narrow, not because it is short.

young.what: Your large intestine is a wide tube that goes around your small intestine.
young.does: It soaks up water from leftover food and turns the rest into poo.
young.funFact: Trillions of friendly bacteria live in your large intestine and help keep you healthy!

junior.what: The large intestine is a wider tube about 1.5 metres long, made of the caecum, colon and rectum.
junior.does: It absorbs water and salts from undigested food and stores the waste until it leaves the body.
junior.funFact: Friendly gut bacteria here make some vitamins, such as vitamin K.
junior.details: The appendix is a small, finger-shaped pouch attached to the start of the large intestine.

young.what: Your pancreas is a soft organ tucked behind your stomach.
young.does: It makes juices that help digest food, and it helps control the sugar in your blood.
young.funFact: It has two big jobs: digestion and sugar control!

junior.what: The pancreas is a long gland lying behind the stomach.
junior.does: It sends digestive enzymes into the small intestine, and small clusters of cells called the islets of Langerhans release the hormones insulin and glucagon to control blood sugar.
junior.funFact: Insulin was first used to treat diabetes in 1922.
junior.details: Because it makes both digestive juices and hormones, the pancreas belongs to two body systems.
